newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Mrs. Clinton, daughter on Tanzanian safari.
newsitem.headline: Mrs. Clinton, daughter on Tanzanian safari.

text.p: It was the hippos soaking in a pond that got Chelsea Clinton's attention on Wednesday on a sightseeing safari adventure with her mother, U.S. First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton.
"Look, look, look! See?" 17-year-old Chelsea said to Mrs. Clinton as they both tried to glimpse the hippos with binoculars when the animals brought their noses up for air.

The Clintons saw hippos, zebras, endangered black rhinos, an elephant with long tusks, and a pride of lions during their five-hour excursion into Ngorongoro Crater, a wildlife-rich conservation area in northern Tanzania.
Mrs. Clinton and her daughter rode in a convoy of four- wheel drive vehicles from their lodge on the crater rim down winding roads of dark-red dirt to the crater floor.

The crater was formed by the collapse of a volcano an estimated 2.5 million years ago. It is now a fertile plain with sweeping grasslands and a wide variety of east African wildlife, including teeming herds of Cape Buffalo, wildebeest and zebras.

The Clintons, enjoying some tourism in the waning days of their two-week tour of Africa, were only about a half hour into their ride when five haughty-looking lions came walking by and paid no attention to the VIP caravan.
Chelsea popped up through the rooftop of her vehicle to look at them with binoculars while her mother watched through the window.
Soon afterward they spied a sleeping black rhino, one of only 17 in the park and guarded by a permanent patrol of rifle-carrying park rangers to protect them from poachers.
There were enough animals to stock a good-sized zoo: ostriches, monkeys, gazelles, even some warthogs -- which bear a resemblance to the Arkansas razorbacks of President Bill Clinton's home state.
"The zebras are beautiful," Mrs. Clinton said at the rest area naer the hippo pond. "I love the way they look and act. The wildebeest are such strange animals."

She said she was impressed by the fact that 25 percent of Tanzania's land has been set aside for national parks. She said she believed Tanzania wants more tourists at Ngorongoro but that the country also wants to maintain control on the number of visitors so as not to harm the environmentally sensitive area.

Mrs. Clinton was to travel to Kampala, Uganda, on Thursday, then visit Eritrea before returning to Washington early on Sunday. She has already visited Senegal, South Africa and Zimbabwe on her six-nation goodwill trip.
